patterns.title: Indentation defines blocks
patterns.explanation: Python uses indentation (not braces) to mark which lines belong inside a block, like the body of an if or for statement.

sentences.error: The body must be indented to belong to the if block.
Indentation levels must be consistent within a block.

patterns.title: if / elif / else structure
patterns.explanation: elif checks another condition only if the previous ones were false. else runs only if none of them were true.
patterns.hint: This checks a second condition, between if and else.

patterns.title: Comparison vs assignment
patterns.explanation: = assigns a value; == checks whether two values are equal. Using = inside an if condition is a common beginner mistake.

sentences.error: = assigns a value; use == to compare.

patterns.title: for loop over a sequence
patterns.explanation: for repeats a block once per item in a sequence. The loop variable is used with the keyword in before the sequence.
patterns.hint: This keyword connects the loop variable to the sequence.

patterns.title: while loop structure
patterns.explanation: while repeats a block as long as its condition stays true. The condition is checked again before every repeat.
patterns.hint: This keyword starts a condition-based loop.

patterns.title: break vs continue
patterns.explanation: break exits the loop completely. continue skips only the rest of the current pass and moves to the next item.

patterns.title: List comprehension structure
patterns.explanation: A list comprehension builds a new list in one line: an expression, followed by a for clause, inside square brackets.

patterns.title: List comprehension with a condition
patterns.explanation: An if clause at the end of a comprehension filters which items are included.
patterns.template: evens = [x for x in numbers ___ x % 2 == 0]
patterns.hint: This keyword filters items in a comprehension.

patterns.title: Function definition structure
patterns.explanation: A function is defined with def, a name, parentheses for parameters, and a colon to start its body.

patterns.title: Default parameter values
patterns.explanation: A parameter can have a default value, used only when the caller doesn't supply that argument.

sentences.error: A default value must follow the = sign.

patterns.title: *args collects extra arguments
patterns.explanation: *args gathers any extra positional arguments into a tuple inside the function.

patterns.title: try / except structure
patterns.explanation: Code that might fail goes in the try block. If an error occurs, Python jumps to the matching except block instead of crashing.
patterns.template:
___:
    result = 10 / 0
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print('cannot divide by zero')
patterns.hint: This keyword marks the risky code block.

patterns.title: finally always runs
patterns.explanation: A finally block runs whether or not an exception occurred — useful for cleanup like closing a file.

sentences.error: else is not for cleanup code; use finally.

patterns.title: Class definition and __init__
patterns.explanation: A class groups data and behavior together. __init__ runs automatically when a new instance is created, to set up its starting state.

patterns.title: self refers to the instance
patterns.explanation: self is the first parameter of every instance method, and refers to the specific object the method was called on.

sentences.error: Instance methods need self as their first parameter.

patterns.title: Inheritance syntax
patterns.explanation: A class inherits from another by naming it in parentheses after the class name, gaining its methods and attributes.
patterns.hint: Parentheses hold the parent class name.

patterns.title: f-string value insertion
patterns.explanation: An f-string lets you embed a variable's value directly inside text using curly braces, right where it belongs.
patterns.hint: This letter before the quotes marks an f-string.

patterns.title: Slice notation [start:stop]
patterns.explanation: A slice selects a range of a sequence. The start index is included; the stop index is not.
patterns.hint: Start and stop are separated by this symbol.

patterns.title: Multiple assignment / unpacking
patterns.explanation: A tuple or list can be unpacked into several variables at once, matched by position.

patterns.title: Safe dictionary lookup
patterns.explanation: Square-bracket access raises an error if the key is missing. .get() returns None (or a default) instead of crashing.

sentences.text: age = person['age']  # key may not exist, risk of crash
sentences.error: Direct indexing raises KeyError if the key is missing; use .get() to be safe.

patterns.title: Dict comprehension structure
patterns.explanation: A dict comprehension builds a dictionary in one line: a key:value pair, followed by a for clause, inside curly braces.

patterns.title: Function type hints
patterns.explanation: A parameter's expected type follows a colon; the function's return type follows an arrow after the parentheses.
patterns.template:
def square(x: int) ___ int:
    return x * x
patterns.hint: This symbol introduces the return type.

patterns.title: Optional means value or None
patterns.explanation: Optional[str] means the value is either a str or None — it documents that None is a valid possibility.

sentences.text:
def find(name: str) -> Optional[int]:
    return None

def find(name: str) -> int:
    return None  # violates the declared return type
sentences.error: The return type says int, but None is returned; Optional[int] would be honest here.

patterns.title: defaultdict avoids key errors
patterns.explanation: defaultdict creates a default value automatically for a missing key instead of raising KeyError.

sentences.text:
counts = {}
counts['a'] += 1  # key doesn't exist yet
sentences.error: A plain dict raises KeyError on a missing key; defaultdict would not.

patterns.title: search vs match
patterns.explanation: re.match only checks the start of the string. re.search looks for the pattern anywhere in the string.

sentences.text: re.search('cat', 'my cat sleeps')  # finds it anywhere
re.match('cat', 'my cat sleeps')  # only checks the start
sentences.error: match only looks at the beginning of the string, so this won't find 'cat' here.

patterns.title: Custom context manager methods
patterns.explanation: __enter__ runs when a with block starts and __exit__ runs when it ends, even if an error occurred.

patterns.title: Catching specific exceptions first
patterns.explanation: More specific exception types should be caught before more general ones, since the first matching except wins.

sentences.error: Exception already catches everything, so the more specific except below it can never run.

patterns.title: Abstract methods must be overridden
patterns.explanation: A method marked @abstractmethod has no usable implementation in the base class — every subclass must provide its own.
patterns.hint: This decorator forces subclasses to implement the method.

patterns.title: __str__ vs __repr__
patterns.explanation: __str__ gives a readable description for users (used by print and str()). __repr__ gives an unambiguous one for developers.

sentences.text:
def __str__(self):
    return f'Person(name={self.name!r})'  # this reads like __repr__

patterns.title: async def and await
patterns.explanation: A coroutine is defined with async def. Inside it, await pauses until another async operation finishes, without blocking the whole program.
patterns.template:
async def fetch_data():
    result = ___ get_from_network()
    return result
patterns.hint: This keyword pauses for an async result.

patterns.title: Coroutines need to be awaited
patterns.explanation: Calling an async function doesn't run it immediately — it returns a coroutine object that must be awaited (or scheduled) to actually execute.

sentences.text: result = fetch_data()  # this is just a coroutine object, not yet run
sentences.error: Calling an async function alone doesn't execute it — it must be awaited.

patterns.title: @dataclass generates boilerplate
patterns.explanation: @dataclass automatically writes __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ for a class based on its annotated fields.
patterns.template:
___
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int
patterns.hint: This decorator auto-generates the class's boilerplate methods.

patterns.title: Slice with a step
patterns.explanation: A third number in a slice sets the step size — how many items to skip between each selected one.
patterns.hint: Start, stop, and step are all separated by this symbol.

patterns.title: Unpacking arguments with *
patterns.explanation: A * before a list or tuple in a function call spreads its items out as separate positional arguments.

sentences.text:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
print(nums)  # prints the list itself, [1, 2, 3]

patterns.title: Generator functions use yield
patterns.explanation: A function containing yield becomes a generator — calling it doesn't run the body immediately, it returns an object that produces values one at a time.

sentences.error: return exits the function immediately on the first loop pass; yield is needed to produce a sequence of values.

patterns.title: Locks prevent race conditions
patterns.explanation: When multiple threads share data, a Lock ensures only one thread modifies it at a time, preventing corrupted results.

sentences.text: balance += amount  # no lock, two threads could interfere
sentences.error: Without a lock, two threads updating balance at once can lose an update.

patterns.title: Method resolution order
patterns.explanation: With multiple inheritance, Python searches parent classes in a specific order (MRO) to decide which method actually runs.
patterns.hint: This attribute shows the class search order.
